title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking sentinel-error matching
rationale: The package still declares ErrNotFound, so callers matching with errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) or == now treat every miss as an unexpected error instead of a not-found condition. Wrap the sentinel (fmt.Errorf("user %q: %w", id, ErrNotFound)) to preserve the contract.

title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking callers that match on the sentinel
rationale: Callers matching the exported ErrNotFound sentinel via errors.Is stop matching, so lookups of missing users are treated as unexpected errors. Wrapping the sentinel with %w preserves the contract.

title: Lookup no longer returns the documented sentinel ErrNotFound
rationale: The sentinel `ErrNotFound` still exists but `Lookup` no longer returns it, so any caller using `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` breaks silently. Wrap the sentinel with `%w` or return it unchanged to preserve the contract.

title: Remaining() silently changes its return unit from bytes to megabytes while the rest of the package API stays in bytes
rationale: New and Record are denominated in bytes, so callers that combine Remaining() with byte values for quota-admission checks will be off by a factor of 2^20 and admit or reject incorrectly. The display need for whole megabytes should be met at the display site or by a distinctly named method such as RemainingMB, not by changing the unit inside the shared byte-denominated accessor.

title: Exported parseDuration now returns seconds instead of milliseconds with an unchanged signature
rationale: The return unit of the exported parseDuration changed by a factor of 1000 while its (string) => number signature is unchanged, so any caller not updated in this same change — for example one passing the result to setTimeout or a millisecond-based TTL — silently gets durations 1000× too short, and the type system cannot flag it. If the unit change is intentional, encode it in the name or return type (e.g. parseDurationSeconds) so remaining millisecond-assuming callers fail visibly instead of at runtime.

title: Guard does not reject negative limit, which SQLite treats as unlimited
rationale: In SQLite, a negative LIMIT is treated as no upper bound, so fetch_orders(conn, 0, -1) returns every row in the table — exactly the outcome the docstring says this guard prevents. The check validates only the upper bound, leaving the documented guarantee unenforced.

title: Guard rejects limit=0, which SQLite handled safely as zero rows
rationale: SQLite treats only a negative LIMIT as unbounded; LIMIT 0 returns zero rows, so a caller passing limit=0 previously got an empty list and now gets a ValueError. The new docstring's justification ("SQLite would otherwise read as 'no limit'") is also factually wrong for the limit=0 case, so the author should either narrow the check to limit < 0 or correct the stated reason while consciously accepting the behavior change for zero.

title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking the sentinel error contract
rationale: Lookup's documented contract was to return ErrNotFound, and callers matching with errors.Is(ErrNotFound) now see a mismatch on every miss. The unmatched callers are not visible here, but ErrNotFound remains exported, so any caller relying on it silently gets a false negative. Wrapping the sentinel preserves errors.Is while adding the id.

title: Exported parseDuration now returns seconds instead of milliseconds, silently changing the value every existing caller receives
rationale: parseDuration is exported, so callers outside this file consume its return value; any caller that passes the result to a millisecond-based API such as setTimeout now receives a value 1000x too small (60x for minutes) with no error raised. The diff shows no call-site updates, so this rests on the assumption that such callers exist and were not migrated to seconds in this same change.

title: Negative limit bypasses the MAX_PAGE guard and fetches the whole table
rationale: SQLite treats a negative LIMIT as unbounded, so a negative limit reaching the query returns every row in the table — the whole-table pull the MAX_PAGE guard exists to prevent. -1 is a common 'no limit' convention among callers, so the range check must include the lower bound, not just cap the upper one.

title: Remaining() changes its return unit from bytes to megabytes for every caller, not just the dashboard
rationale: New and Record are byte-denominated, so Remaining() was the type's byte accessor; after this change every caller receives whole megabytes. Any caller comparing the result against a byte count (for example, admission control before Record) would silently get a value 2^20 times smaller, though no such caller appears in the shown code; the megabyte conversion belongs at the display site or in a separate method, leaving Remaining() in bytes.

title: Negative limit bypasses the MAX_PAGE guard and returns the whole table
rationale: SQLite treats a negative LIMIT as unbounded, so fetch_orders(conn, 0, -1) returns every row in the table — the exact outcome this guard was added to prevent. The check only rejects limits above MAX_PAGE, so a caller whose limit comes from arithmetic that can go negative silently defeats it.

title: Remaining() now returns truncated megabytes instead of bytes, changing the method's contract
rationale: New and Record deal in bytes, so a caller still comparing Remaining() against a byte count (e.g. admission control against a file size) would get a value 2^20 times smaller and truncated toward zero, with no compile-time signal. That breakage assumes callers outside the shown change; if only the dashboard needs whole megabytes, a separate display helper would preserve the byte contract.

title: Remaining() changes its return unit from bytes to megabytes on a byte-based API
rationale: The type is documented as tracking a byte allowance, New takes bytes, and Record charges bytes, but Remaining now returns whole MiB, so the package's units are inconsistent and any caller that uses the return value as a byte count (for example, to decide whether an upload of n bytes fits) is silently off by a factor of 2^20. No callers of this exported method are shown, so the consequence rests on the assumption that a byte-consuming caller exists; if only the dashboard reads this value, converting at the display layer or adding a RemainingMiB method would preserve the byte contract.
